questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis for 2 weeks. The ulcer has a clean base with indurated edges. Dark-field microscopy of the ulcer exudate shows motile spiral organisms. Which is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Treponema pallidum causes primary syphilis. The classic chancre is painless with indurated edges, and dark-field microscopy demonstrates the motile spirochetes. Haemophilus ducreyi causes painful chancroid with soft edges.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman develops erythema, scaling, and fissuring of the web spaces between toes along with onychomycosis. KOH examination shows septate hyphae. The most common causative organism is:
questions.exp: Trichophyton rubrum is the most common dermatophyte worldwide and the predominant cause of tinea pedis and onychomycosis. It produces septate hyphae on KOH examination.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on MDT develops sudden onset facial erythema, fever, and multiple tender erythematous nodules over the body. Nerve function is intact. This reaction is classified as:
questions.exp: Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL) is a Type 2 lepra reaction seen in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous leprosy. It presents with tender erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic features. It is an immune complex (Type III hypersensitivity) mediated reaction.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on normal and erythematous skin, predominantly on flexural areas. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition at the dermoepidermal junction. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid shows tense bullae on erythematous skin with linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ on DIF. The target antigens are BPAG2 (BP180/type XVII collagen) and BPAG1 (BP230). Pemphigus shows intercellular IgG in a chicken-wire pattern.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base at the elbows and scalp. Skin biopsy shows subepidermal vesicles with neutrophilic infiltrate at the tips of dermal papillae. IgA deposits are found at dermal papillae on DIF. The most appropriate treatment is:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring's disease) is characterised by IgA deposits at dermal papillae and is associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy. Dapsone provides rapid relief of itch and blistering. A gluten-free diet is the definitive long-term treatment.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with hypopigmented anaesthetic patches on the trunk. Slit-skin smear is negative. Biopsy shows epithelioid cell granulomas with Langhans giant cells involving the neurovascular bundles. The nerve twigs within the granuloma show:
questions.exp: In tuberculoid leprosy (TT), the granuloma extends into and destroys the nerve twigs — nerve fibres are not identifiable within the granuloma. This nerve destruction accounts for the anaesthesia seen clinically.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with a solitary pearly nodule on the nose with telangiectasia and central ulceration. The most common histological subtype of this tumour is:
questions.exp: Nodular basal cell carcinoma is the most common subtype (~60-80%), presenting as a pearly/translucent nodule with telangiectasia that may ulcerate centrally (rodent ulcer). Morphoeic BCC carries the worst prognosis due to aggressive infiltration.

questions.q: A 65-year-old woman develops tightening of facial skin, Raynaud's phenomenon, and dysphagia. ANA is positive with an anticentromere antibody pattern. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Anticentromere antibody (ACA) is strongly associated with limited systemic sclerosis/CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Oesophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia). Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse SSc.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with a butterfly-shaped erythema on the face, photosensitivity, and oral ulcers. ANA is positive at 1:640 and anti-dsDNA antibody is positive. Which complement pathway is primarily activated in SLE?
questions.exp: In SLE, immune complexes activate complement predominantly via the classical pathway (C1q binds immune complexes). Low C3 and C4 reflect complement consumption. C4 levels are particularly informative for disease activity.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with well-demarcated silvery-white scaly plaques on the elbows, scalp, and knees with nail pitting and onycholysis. The pathological hallmark on histology is:
questions.exp: Psoriasis classically shows regular acanthosis, elongated rete ridges, parakeratosis (with loss of granular layer), dilated tortuous papillary capillaries, Munro's microabscesses (neutrophils in parakeratotic stratum corneum), and Kogoj's spongiform pustules.

questions.q: A 19-year-old develops severe photosensitivity, vesicles on sun-exposed areas, hypertrichosis, and port-wine–coloured urine. Urine fluorescence under Wood's lamp is pink-red. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is the most common porphyria, caused by uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency. It presents with skin fragility, blisters on sun-exposed areas, hypertrichosis, and urine shows pink-red fluorescence due to excess uroporphyrin.

questions.q: A patient on dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis develops haemolytic anaemia with Heinz bodies on peripheral smear. The patient is most likely deficient in:
questions.exp: Dapsone causes methaemoglobinaemia and haemolytic anaemia, which is particularly severe in G6PD-deficient patients. G6PD is critical for the hexose monophosphate shunt that generates NADPH to protect RBCs from oxidative stress. Heinz bodies represent denatured haemoglobin precipitates.

questions.q: A 32-year-old HIV-positive man presents with multiple violaceous papules and plaques on skin, hard palate, and lower extremities. CD4 count is 120 cells/μL. Biopsy shows spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces and extravasated RBCs. The causative virus is:
questions.exp: Kaposi's sarcoma in HIV patients is caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8/KSHV). It typically occurs with CD4 <200 cells/μL. Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and PAS-positive hyaline globules.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Culture grows Staphylococcus aureus. The most appropriate topical antibiotic for localised disease is:
questions.exp: Mupirocin (pseudomonic acid) is the first-line topical antibiotic for localised impetigo. It inhibits bacterial isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase and is effective against MRSA. For widespread disease, oral antibiotics (cefalexin or amoxicillin-clavulanate) are used.

questions.q: A 28-year-old presents with well-defined hypopigmented macules on the trunk. Wood's lamp examination shows chalky-white fluorescence. KOH preparation shows a 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. The treatment of choice is:
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur. KOH shows short hyphae and spores ('spaghetti and meatballs'). Topical selenium sulphide, ketoconazole, or zinc pyrithione are first-line. Oral itraconazole is used for extensive disease. Griseofulvin is NOT effective against Malassezia.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child develops scattered umbilicated pearly papules on the trunk and face. The child attends a swimming class. The lesions are caused by a poxvirus. The preferred management in an immunocompetent child is:
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum in immunocompetent children is self-limiting and often resolves spontaneously. Watchful waiting is preferred; curettage is used if treatment is needed. Acyclovir is ineffective against poxviruses.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man has an asymmetric, irregularly pigmented lesion with variegated colours on the back. Excision biopsy confirms melanoma with Breslow thickness 0.6 mm. The recommended surgical excision margin is:
questions.exp: For melanoma with Breslow thickness ≤1.0 mm, the recommended surgical excision margin is 1 cm. For 1.01–2 mm the margin is 1–2 cm; for >2 mm it is 2 cm. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is considered for lesions >0.8 mm.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman develops diffuse non-scarring hair loss 3 months after typhoid fever. Pull test is positive. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Telogen effluvium presents as diffuse non-scarring hair loss 2–4 months after a triggering event (fever, surgery, childbirth, stress). Follicles prematurely enter telogen phase. Pull test is positive (>6 telogen hairs per pull). It is usually self-limiting.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman has bilateral malar hyperpigmentation worsening in summer and aggravated by OCP use. Wood's lamp shows enhancement of the pigmentation. The pigment is located in the:
questions.exp: Wood's lamp (365 nm UV) enhances epidermal pigmentation (greater contrast) but does not enhance dermal pigmentation. Epidermal melasma responds better to treatment. The mixed type shows partial enhancement.

questions.q: A 45-year-old presents with chronic eczematous dermatitis on hands and feet since childhood, associated with asthma and allergic rhinitis. Serum IgE is markedly elevated. The skin barrier defect is due to mutation in:
questions.exp: Loss-of-function mutations in the filaggrin (FLG) gene are the strongest known genetic risk factor for atopic dermatitis. Filaggrin is essential for skin barrier function and natural moisturising factor production. Its deficiency leads to increased transepidermal water loss and allergen penetration.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man with HIV has painless genital warts (condylomata acuminata). The HPV types most commonly responsible are:
questions.exp: Condylomata acuminata are caused predominantly by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11 (~90% of cases). HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk types associated with cervical and anal carcinoma. HPV 1 and 2 cause common warts.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man has recurrent painful grouped vesicles on the glans penis recurring every 6–8 weeks. PCR confirms HSV-2. The appropriate suppressive therapy is:
opts: Acyclovir 200 mg five times daily for 5 days
questions.exp: For frequent recurrences of genital herpes (≥6 per year), daily suppressive therapy with valacyclovir 500 mg OD (or acyclovir 400 mg BD) is recommended. This reduces recurrence frequency by ~70–80% and decreases transmission risk.

questions.q: A 55-year-old farmer develops a painless black eschar surrounded by marked oedema on the forearm after handling animal hides. Gram stain of exudate shows large gram-positive bacilli in chains. The treatment of choice is:
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax (caused by Bacillus anthracis) is treated with ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 7–10 days (first-line), or oral penicillin if susceptible. IV antibiotics are used for systemic disease. Oedema management is supportive.

questions.q: During PUVA therapy a 38-year-old psoriasis patient develops phototoxic erythema. The mechanism of action of psoralen in PUVA is:
opts: Formation of cyclobutane photoadducts with DNA
questions.exp: Psoralens (8-MOP, 5-MOP) intercalate into DNA and, upon UVA (320–400 nm) activation, form covalent cyclobutane monoadducts and cross-links (diadducts) with thymine residues. This inhibits DNA replication and exerts anti-proliferative and immunomodulatory effects.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man with donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) has a biopsy showing large mononuclear cells with intracytoplasmic bacteria. The characteristic histological finding is called:
questions.exp: Donovanosis (caused by Klebsiella granulomatis) is diagnosed by demonstrating Donovan bodies — intracytoplasmic clusters of organisms (coccobacilli with bipolar 'safety pin' staining) within large mononuclear cells on Giemsa or Warthin-Starry silver stain.

questions.q: A neonate develops epidermolysis bullosa with scarring and milia formation. Electron microscopy shows blister formation beneath the lamina densa. The protein most likely deficient is:
questions.exp: Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB) is caused by mutations in COL7A1 encoding type VII collagen, the major component of anchoring fibrils below the lamina densa. EM shows blister below the lamina densa with absent/reduced anchoring fibrils. Scarring and milia are hallmarks of DEB.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman started on methotrexate for severe psoriasis. Which investigation is most important to monitor during long-term therapy?
opts: LFTs and hepatic fibrosis markers (PIIINP/ELF score)
questions.exp: Methotrexate is hepatotoxic with cumulative dose-related risk of fibrosis and cirrhosis. Current guidelines recommend LFTs every 4–8 weeks, PIIINP/ELF score monitoring, and liver biopsy when cumulative dose exceeds 1.5 g or with abnormal fibrosis markers.

questions.q: A 20-year-old man presents with tinea capitis showing black dots (broken hair stubs) and patchy alopecia. There is no fluorescence under Wood's lamp. The most likely causative organism is:
questions.exp: Trichophyton tonsurans causes endothrix tinea capitis (spores inside hair shaft), presenting with the black dot pattern (hair breaks at scalp level). It does NOT fluoresce under Wood's lamp. Microsporum species cause ectothrix infection and show green fluorescence. T. schoenleinii causes favus.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man develops a painful vesicular eruption along the right T5 dermatome. He subsequently develops severe burning pain persisting for 4 months after the rash resolves. The mechanism underlying this complication is:
opts: Peripheral and central sensitisation after neuronal injury and Wallerian degeneration
Secondary bacterial infection of the nerve
questions.exp: Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) — pain persisting >3 months after herpes zoster — results from VZV-induced damage to sensory neurons, Wallerian degeneration, and subsequent peripheral and central sensitisation. It occurs in ~30% of patients over 60 years.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man with borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy on MDT develops sudden wrist drop and clawing of the ring and little fingers. The most important immediate management is:
opts: Surgical decompression of the ulnar nerve
questions.exp: Sudden nerve function impairment in leprosy (Type 1 reaction or silent neuropathy) requires urgent corticosteroid therapy — prednisolone starting at 40–60 mg/day (approximately 1 mg/kg/day) — to reduce inflammation and prevent permanent nerve damage. Early treatment within 6 months gives best recovery.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman develops recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and hypopyon uveitis. Pathergy test is positive. HLA typing shows HLA-B51. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Behcet's disease is a systemic vasculitis characterised by the triad of recurrent oral aphthae, genital ulcers, and ocular inflammation (hypopyon uveitis). Positive pathergy test and HLA-B51 association are characteristic. It is most prevalent along the ancient Silk Road.
